--- title: "Writing a Paper" engine: knitr --- ## What a paper needs A paper needs things a report doesn't: - Citations and a reference list in a required style - Numbered figures and tables you can refer to in the text - An abstract - No visible code
And usually a [Word]{.uwred} file: - Co-authors edit it with track changes - Many journals ask for `.docx` -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## Start from your report In the terminal, in your `mendota_ice` folder: ```bash cp report.qmd paper.qmd ```
- `cp` copies a file: first the original, then the new name - `paper.qmd` starts with everything your report has
Copying is fine for today, but now the same code lives in three files: report, slides, and paper. - Change one, and you must remember to change the other - The DRY unit shows how to keep the code in one place -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## A paper's YAML header Replace the YAML header at the top of `paper.qmd`: ```yaml --- title: "Ice Cover on Lake Mendota" author: "Your Name" date: today abstract: | Lake Mendota freezes for fewer days each winter than it did in the 1800s. We summarize more than 170 years of ice records. format: docx execute: echo: false --- ```
- `abstract: |` starts a block; the indented lines below it are the abstract - `format: docx` builds a Word document - `execute:` `echo: false` hides all code; readers see only the results - No `embed-resources` needed; a Word file always holds its own figures -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## Render to Word ```bash quarto render paper.qmd ```
Quarto writes [`paper.docx`]{.uwred} next to your `.qmd`. - Open it in Word (or Google Docs, or LibreOffice)
You should see: - The abstract under the title - Your sections, sentences, and figure - No code
On Windows, close `paper.docx` in Word before you render again. - Word locks open files, so Quarto can't replace it -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## Citations need a `.bib` file You downloaded `refs.bib` during setup. It holds one entry (shortened here): ```bibtex @dataset{magnuson2026, author = {Magnuson, J. J. and Carpenter, S. R. and Stanley, E. H.}, title = {{North Temperate Lakes LTER}: Ice Duration - ...}, year = {2026}, publisher = {Environmental Data Initiative}, doi = {10.6073/pasta/6a95bee73799927cbafbf87393be7038}, ... } ```
- `magnuson2026` is the [citation key]{.uwred}; you cite the source with it - Get entries from Google Scholar (Cite → BibTeX), a journal's "Export citation" link, or Zotero
Point your paper to the file; add to the YAML header: ```yaml bibliography: refs.bib ``` -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## Citation style Quarto's default style is Chicago author-date. - For APA, add one more line to the YAML header: ```yaml bibliography: refs.bib csl: apa.csl ```
A [CSL]{.uwred} (Citation Style Language) file describes one style. - You downloaded `apa.csl` during setup, next to `refs.bib` - Thousands of styles, including many journals, are at - For another style, download its `.csl` file into your repo and change the `csl:` line -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## Cite a source In your Background section, add a citation to the first sentence: ```markdown Lake Mendota has been watched for ice since the **1850s** [@magnuson2026]. ```
| You type | Quarto writes | |---|---| | `[@magnuson2026]` | (Magnuson et al., 2026) | | `@magnuson2026` | Magnuson et al. (2026) |
At the very end of `paper.qmd`, add a heading: ```markdown ## References ``` - Quarto puts the reference list there, formatted in APA -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## Number the figure Change the figure chunk's label and add a caption: ```{{r}} #| label: fig-ice_days #| fig-cap: "Days of ice cover on Lake Mendota, by winter." ice |> ggplot(aes(x = year, y = ice_days)) + geom_line() + labs(x = "Winter (year it ended)", y = "Days of ice cover") + theme_minimal() ```
Then refer to it in a sentence: ```markdown Ice cover has declined since the 1850s (@fig-ice_days). ``` - The label must start with `fig-`; Quarto requires that hyphen (the rest stays snake_case) - Quarto numbers the figure and writes "Figure 1" for you -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## Add a numbered table Add a new chunk: ```{{r}} #| label: tbl-periods #| tbl-cap: "Ice cover by half century." ice |> group_by(half_century = floor(year / 50) * 50) |> summarize(winters = n(), mean_days = round(mean(ice_days))) |> knitr::kable() ```
Then refer to it in a sentence: ```markdown @tbl-periods shows the average for each half century. ``` - Same pattern as figures: a `tbl-` label, a `tbl-cap` caption - `knitr::kable()` turns a data frame into a table that works in Word, PDF, and HTML -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## Your turn ::: {.callout-wide} ::: {.callout-important} # Try it 1. Add `bibliography:` and `csl:` to your YAML header 2. Cite `@magnuson2026` in your Background section, and add `## References` at the end 3. Give your figure a `fig-` label and a caption, and refer to it in a sentence 4. Add the table chunk, and refer to it in a sentence 5. Render, and open `paper.docx` ::: ::: -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## Your turn: check your paper In `paper.docx`, look for (Magnuson et al., 2026), Figure 1, Table 1, and the reference list.
A typo doesn't stop the render. - Quarto prints a [WARNING]{.uwred} in the terminal and keeps going - Read the render output, not just the Word file
| You see | Fix | |---|---| | `(magnuson?)` | The key doesn't match `refs.bib`; check spelling and the `bibliography:` line | | `?@fig-ice_days` | The label and the reference must match exactly, and start with `fig-` | | Code in the Word file | Check the indentation of `echo: false` under `execute:` | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## Word and PDF from one render ```yaml format: docx: default typst: citeproc: true ```
`quarto render paper.qmd` now makes both `paper.docx` and `paper.pdf`. - `default` means "no extra options for this format" - Typst makes the PDF, with no LaTeX needed
Why `citeproc: true`? - Typst formats citations itself, and its APA output differs a little from Word's - This tells it to use the same citation engine as the Word file -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## Where we are We have: - Turned the report into a paper with a few YAML changes - Cited a source, with a reference list in APA style - Numbered a figure and a table, and referred to them in the text - Rendered to Word (and PDF)
::: {.callout-wide} ::: {.callout-important} # Where to go next The [Advanced]{.uwred} units in the book (no slides) pick up from here. - Keep editing your own report, slides, and paper, and render them to see each new feature - Topics include more markdown, chunk options and figures, tables, slide formatting, YAML in depth, Quarto projects, and Git - Also: how to keep [one copy of your code]{.uwred} for a report, slides, and a paper ::: :::
